title: Fibrations and weak equivalences of quasicategories in the Joyal model structure
statement: Use quasicategories, inner horns, equivalence edges, functor simplicial sets and functor equivalences as defined in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Use the Joyal model structure and its classes of fibrations and weak equivalences from [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]. For any two quasicategories $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$ in the same universe and any simplicial functor $f:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$, the following characterizations hold. (1) The map $f$ is a Joyal fibration if and only if it has the right lifting property against every inner horn $\Lambda_i^n\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$, $0<i<n$, and, for every vertex $c\in\mathcal C$ and equivalence edge $e:f(c)\to d$ in $\mathcal D$, there is an equivalence edge $\widetilde e:c\to\widetilde d$ in $\mathcal C$ with $f(\widetilde e)=e$. (2) The map $f$ is a Joyal weak equivalence if and only if it has a simplicial quasi-inverse $g:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ and coherent natural equivalences between $gf$ and $\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}$ and between $fg$ and $\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal D}$, where these are equivalence edges in the corresponding functor quasicategories. In (2) the Joyal weak equivalences are exactly the categorical equivalences defined by the tests $h\operatorname{Fun}(-,\mathcal E)$ in [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure].

source.place: Cisinski, Higher Categories and Homotopical Algebra, revision July 30, 2026: Definition 3.3.15 (printed p.97); Theorem 3.6.1 (printed pp.112-113); Remark 3.6.5 and Corollary 3.6.6 (printed p.114); Theorem 3.6.8 (printed pp.115-116) identifies the hFun test definition of categorical equivalence. Read the already available Q26/cisinski.txt reference copy; not archived in literature/. WANTED: archived source. No Stacks tag states these quasicategorical characterizations. Second reader independently opened the online PDF on 2026-10-17 at PDF pages 113,128-131 (printed pp.97,112-116) and checked both directions, including source-prescribed equivalence lifting and the hFun test convention.

proof.text: First record the elementary equivalence-edge consequence of [lem-coef-quasicategory-edge-triangle-presentation]. In any quasicategory $Q$, an equivalence edge gives an isomorphism in $hQ$ by its two inverse triangles. Conversely, if $[u]$ is invertible, represent its inverse by an edge $v$ using that node, and realize both equations $[v][u]=1$ and $[u][v]=1$ by its triangle clause. The SAME edge $v$ then supplies both inverse triangles of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Thus an isomorphism in $hQ$ can always be represented by an equivalence edge with the exact prescribed vertices. Any simplicial map preserves equivalence edges: apply it to the edge, its inverse, and the two triangles.

source.place: Theorem 1.6.6 and Corollary 1.6.8, with the equivalence-edge consequence derived explicitly.

proof.text: Let $J,a,b,c,s_{\varepsilon,n}$ be the explicit interval and tests of [lem-coef-joyal-interval-boundary-tests]. In $hJ$ the two attaching triangles give $[b][a]=1_0$ and $[a][c]=1_1$; hence $[b]=[b][a][c]=[c]$, and all three generating edges are invertible. Now suppose $f:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ is a Joyal fibration. The current statement of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure] makes every inner horn a trivial cofibration and characterizes fibrations by right lifting against trivial cofibrations. Applying that lifting assertion gives every inner-horn lift for $f$. For an equivalence $u:f(x)\to y$, use its inverse twice and its two inverse triangles to define a simplicial map $J\to\mathcal D$ whose distinguished edge $a$ is $u$. There is a square with left side $s_{0,0}:\{0\}\to J$, top vertex $x$, and right side $f$. This map is a trivial cofibration by the interval-test node, so the model lifting axiom gives $J\to\mathcal C$ over the prescribed map to $\mathcal D$. Its edge $a$ starts at exactly $x$ and maps to exactly $u$. Its class is invertible because the functor $hJ\to h\mathcal C$ preserves the displayed inverse equations. Step 1 makes that edge an equivalence, proving the forward direction of (1).

source.place: Construction 3.3.1 and Remark 3.3.17; the inverse equations, prescribed source and exact edge equality are written out.

proof.text:
For the converse of (1), assume $f$ lifts all inner horns and all equivalence edges with the prescribed source. It is therefore an isofibration in the precise definition of [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-exponentiation]. Fix $n\geq0$ and $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$, and put $A=\partial\Delta^n$, $B=\Delta^n$. That node applied to $A\hookrightarrow B$ gives an isofibration between quasicategories
$$q:S=\operatorname{Fun}(B,\mathcal C)\longrightarrow T=\operatorname{Fun}(A,\mathcal C)\times_{\operatorname{Fun}(A,\mathcal D)}\operatorname{Fun}(B,\mathcal D).$$
A lifting square against $s_{\varepsilon,n}$ of [lem-coef-joyal-interval-boundary-tests] consists of compatible maps $A\times J\to\mathcal C$, $B\to\mathcal C$ at endpoint $\varepsilon$, and $B\times J\to\mathcal D$. Currying gives a map $v:J\to T$ and a vertex $s\in S$ with $q(s)=v(\varepsilon)$. The inverse equations in $hJ$ from step 2 make every edge of $J$ invertible in $hJ$. Applying $hv$ and step 1 in the quasicategory $T$ shows that every edge of $J$ maps to an equivalence in $T$. Thus $v$ factors through the core $T^\simeq$ as defined in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]: every edge of the image of every simplex is an equivalence. The vertex $s$ belongs to $S^\simeq$, since this core contains all vertices. Consequently the curried square is a square from $\{\varepsilon\}\hookrightarrow J$ to $q^\simeq:S^\simeq\to T^\simeq$.

source.place: Theorem 3.6.1, interval lifting argument; here the already available exponential isofibration is restricted to cores. The factorization of J through the core is proved from the explicit inverse equations, without an identification of a pullback core.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-infinity-core-kan-fibration] to the isofibration $q$ from step 3. It says exactly that $q^\simeq:S^\simeq\to T^\simeq$ is a Kan fibration. It therefore lifts the endpoint inclusion $\{\varepsilon\}\to J$, which is Kan anodyne by [lem-coef-joyal-interval-boundary-tests]. The lifting assertion follows directly from the definition of Kan anodyneness: right lifting holds for horn generators by the Kan-fibration definition in [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-exponentiation]; for a pushout translate a square to its attaching map and glue the lift; along a transfinite chain choose compatible lifts at successor stages and use their colimit at limit stages; for a retract compose with the section square, lift, then compose with the retraction. Isomorphisms lift using inverses. This produces a map $J\to S^\simeq\subseteq\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^n,\mathcal C)$. Uncurrying it gives $\Delta^n\times J\to\mathcal C$ whose restrictions equal both prescribed pieces and whose composite with $f$ is the prescribed base map. Currying sends a degree-$r$ simplex $j:\Delta^r\to J$ to restriction along $1\times j$; evaluation is its inverse, and both commute with operators. Thus $f$ lifts every $s_{\varepsilon,n}$ as well as the assumed inner horns. The fibration test of the interval node proves $f$ is a Joyal fibration. At $n=0$ the boundary is empty and the same square and corner formula still apply.

source.place: Proposition 4.4.3.7, applied to the existing exponential-corner isofibration; interval recognition is Cisinski Remark 3.3.4 and Theorem 2.4.19. Kan-anodyne lifting closure and uncurrying are written explicitly.

proof.text:
For (2), first assume $f$ is a Joyal weak equivalence. Use the current convention of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]: its simplicial sets, inner horns and quasicategories are those of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], and its weak equivalences are the categorical equivalences defined by the generated $h$ and the displayed $h\operatorname{Fun}$ tests. Thus, for every quasicategory $E$, the ordinary functor
$$F_E=f^*:h\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal D,E)\longrightarrow h\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,E)$$
is an equivalence. The internal functor simplicial sets used here are quasicategories: apply the final restriction assertion of [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-exponentiation] to the inclusion $\varnothing\hookrightarrow K$ for the required shape $K$. Essential surjectivity of $F_{\mathcal C}$ at $1_{\mathcal C}$ gives a simplicial map $g:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ and an isomorphism $[gf]\to[1_{\mathcal C}]$ in $h\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal C)$. Step 1 represents it by an actual equivalence edge $\eta:gf\to1_{\mathcal C}$. Postcomposition with $f$ gives an equivalence edge $f\eta:fgf\to f$ in $\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)$, since postcomposition is simplicial and preserves both inverse triangles.

source.place: Theorem 3.6.8 (iii) and Corollary 3.6.6; explicit two-test Yoneda argument replaces a bare citation of their conclusion.

proof.text: Full faithfulness of $F_{\mathcal D}$ now supplies the unique morphism $\alpha:fg\to1_{\mathcal D}$ in $h\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal D,\mathcal D)$ whose restriction is $[f\eta]$, because $F_{\mathcal D}(fg)=fgf$ and $F_{\mathcal D}(1_{\mathcal D})=f$. Lift $[f\eta]^{-1}$ by fullness in the reverse hom set to $\beta:1_{\mathcal D}\to fg$. Their composites restrict to identities; faithfulness gives $\beta\alpha=1_{fg}$ and $\alpha\beta=1_{1_{\mathcal D}}$. Thus $\alpha$ is an isomorphism. Apply step 1 in the quasicategory $\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal D,\mathcal D)$ to represent it by an equivalence edge $\epsilon:fg\to1_{\mathcal D}$. The map $g$ and the edges $\eta,\epsilon$ are exactly the coherent quasi-inverse data of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. No triangle identities beyond those in the definition of each equivalence edge have been imposed.

source.place: Theorem 3.6.8 (iii) implies coherent quasi-invertibility for quasicategories; full faithfulness and both inverse equations are explicit.

proof.text:
Conversely, suppose $g,\eta:gf\simeq1_{\mathcal C}$ and $\epsilon:fg\simeq1_{\mathcal D}$ are the stipulated data, orienting the equivalence edges as displayed by taking their inverses when necessary. Fix any quasicategory $E$ in a sufficiently large universe. Restriction gives functors $f^*:h\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal D,E)\to h\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,E)$ and $g^*$ in the reverse direction. For a diagram $H:\mathcal D\to E$, postcomposition of $\epsilon$ with $H$ gives an equivalence edge $Hfg\to H$. For a diagram $L:\mathcal C\to E$, postcomposition of $\eta$ gives an equivalence edge $Lgf\to L$. These edges vary coherently: for example the first family is adjoint to the simplicial map
$$\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal D,E)\times\Delta^1\longrightarrow\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal D,E),\qquad (H,t)\longmapsto H\circ\epsilon_t,$$
where evaluation is degreewise evaluation and $\epsilon$ is viewed as $\mathcal D\times\Delta^1\to\mathcal D$. To check ordinary naturality, apply this map to an edge $H\to H'$ times $\Delta^1$. The two triangles of $\Delta^1\times\Delta^1$ identify the two composites round its square in the category generated by triangle relations. This proves naturality on edge generators; it then holds on composites and the defining quotient relations. Each component is invertible in $h$ by its inverse triangles. The same construction using $\eta$ on $\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,E)$ gives a natural isomorphism $f^*g^*\cong1$, while $\epsilon$ gives $g^*f^*\cong1$. Hence $f^*$ is an equivalence of ordinary categories for every such $E$, exactly the test in [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]. Therefore $f$ is a Joyal weak equivalence. This also proves the final sentence of (2), with the given hFun convention, rather than requiring a further identification theorem.

source.place: Remark 3.6.5, Corollary 3.6.6 and Theorem 3.6.8, with the hFun implication proved directly by whiskering and the two prism triangles.
